title: Numbers, age & quantities
goal: Count, give your age, ask 'how many / how much', and use ordinals and the special fractions.
intro:
Urdu numbers 1–100 are notoriously irregular — every number from 11 to 99 has its own form (see the **Numbers** chart), and you will learn them gradually by use. Start with 1–20, the tens and the numbers you need for prices and ages.

Urdu also has special, very common words for fractions — **ڈیڑھ** (1½), **ڈھائی** (2½), **ساڑھے** (+½), **سوا** (+¼) and **پونے** (−¼) — used for time, money and quantities.

vocab.note: کتنا / کتنی / کتنے — agrees with the noun.
f. Also a man's name ʿUmar (different vowel).
پونے تین = 2¾. Alone, پونا paunā = three quarters.
m. 'Number' as in phone number, house number, marks.
m. Fruit like bananas is often sold by the dozen.

phrases.native: آپ کا فون نمبر کیا ہے؟
phrases.roman: āp kā fon nambar kyā hai?

phrases.native: میں پہلی بار پاکستان آیا ہوں۔
phrases.roman: maiṃ pahlī bār Pākistān āyā hūṃ.
phrases.en: It's my first time in Pakistan. (man)

grammar.title: Numbers with nouns; asking 'how many / how much'
grammar.body:
A number goes **before** the noun, and the noun takes its plural form (Unit 3): ایک لڑکا, دو لڑکے; ایک کتاب, تین کتابیں. Some masculine nouns don't change: دو سال, پانچ آدمی.

'How many/how much' is **کتنا**, which agrees like an adjective: **کتنا** with masc. singular (uncountable) nouns (کتنا پانی 'how much water'), **کتنی** with feminine nouns (کتنی چائے, کتنی کتابیں), **کتنے** with masc. plurals (کتنے لوگ, کتنے پیسے).

For prices, Urdu asks 'of how much is it?': یہ کتنے کا ہے؟ (کتنے کی if the item is feminine). 'Both' is دونوں; 'all three' is تینوں.

examples.en: How many children do you have?

grammar.title: Age, ordinals and fractions
grammar.body:
**Age** is 'X years of': میں بیس سال کا ہوں (man), میں بیس سال کی ہوں (woman). Ask with آپ کی عمر کیا ہے؟ or, more casually, آپ کتنے سال کے ہیں؟

**Ordinals** are adjectives: پہلا، دوسرا، تیسرا، چوتھا، then add -vāṃ: پانچواں، ساتواں (6th is irregular چھٹا). They agree: پہلا دن, پہلی بار, پانچویں منزل (fifth floor, feminine).

**Fractions**: آدھا ½, ڈیڑھ 1½, ڈھائی 2½. From three on: ساڑھے + number = +½ (ساڑھے تین 3½), سوا + number = +¼ (سوا چار 4¼), پونے + number = −¼ (پونے پانچ 4¾). With hundreds and thousands too: ڈیڑھ سو = 150, ڈھائی ہزار = 2500.

dialogue.title: At the fruit stall
dialogue.setting: Sara buys fruit from a fruit seller (پھل والا) in Rawalpindi.

lines.speaker: Sara
lines.en: Brother, how much are the bananas?

lines.speaker: Sara
lines.native: اچھا، ایک درجن دیجیے۔ اور آم؟
lines.roman: achchhā, ek darjan dījiye. aur ām?
lines.en: OK, give me a dozen. And the mangoes?

lines.speaker: Seller
lines.native: آم تین سو روپے کلو ہیں۔ کتنے دوں؟
lines.roman: ām tīn sau rupe kilo haiṃ. kitne dūṃ?
lines.en: Mangoes are 300 a kilo. How many shall I give you?

lines.speaker: Sara
lines.native: ڈھائی کلو۔ نہیں، دو کلو کافی ہیں۔
lines.roman: ḍhā’ī kilo. nahīṃ, do kilo kāfī haiṃ.
lines.en: Two and a half kilos. No, two kilos is enough.

lines.speaker: Seller
lines.native: ٹھیک ہے۔ کل ساڑھے سات سو روپے۔
lines.roman: ṭhīk hai. kul sāṛhe sāt sau rupe.

lines.speaker: Seller
lines.native: اور یہ ڈھائی سو واپس۔ شکریہ!
lines.roman: aur ye ḍhā’ī sau vāpas. shukriya!

culture: Large numbers in Pakistan and India are counted in **lakhs** (لاکھ, 100,000) and **crores** (کروڑ, 10 million), and written with commas accordingly: 1,00,000. Prices are in rupees (روپیہ, often pronounced 'rupe' in the plural); the paisa is now just a word for money in general (پیسے). Asking someone's age is not rude in Pakistan, and many conversations with new acquaintances include it early on.
